properties.title: Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas (1776)
properties.label: Provincias Internas
properties.description: To defend the northern frontier against Apache and Comanche raiding and foreign rivals, José de Gálvez, now Minister of the Indies, had the northern provinces (Nueva Vizcaya, Sonora y Sinaloa, the Californias, New Mexico, Coahuila and Texas) removed from the viceroy's military authority and placed under a commandant general. The first, Teodoro de Croix, nephew of the former viceroy the Marqués de Croix, took office in 1777 and made Arizpe in Sonora his capital. The command was divided and reunited several times (three districts in 1786, east and west in 1787, reunited and centred on Chihuahua from 1792–93, split again in 1813), which shows how hard the north was to govern from any single point.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Sonora, Sinaloa, Chihuahua, Durango, Coahuila, Baja California, Baja California Sur, Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California, so it shows the claim, not the area Spain controlled. Spanish settlement was confined to river valleys, mining districts, missions and presidios; most of Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and the interior of California was held by independent Apache, Comanche, Navajo, Ute, Quechan and other nations, and Alta California was only occupied from 1769, along the coast. Modern Texas also includes land then in Nuevo Santander and Coahuila (south of the Nueces) and El Paso, then part of New Mexico; Saltillo and Parras passed from Nueva Vizcaya to Coahuila only in 1785. Nuevo León and Nuevo Santander, not included in 1776, were attached to the eastern command in 1786–93 and again from 1812–13.

sources.citation: Luis Navarro García, Don José de Gálvez y la Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas del Norte de Nueva España (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, Sevilla, 1964).

properties.title: Intendancy of México (1786)
properties.label: México
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; this was the largest and richest, governed from the viceregal capital. Besides the Valley of Mexico it took in the mines of Pachuca, Real del Monte and Taxco, the sugar estates of Cuernavaca and Cuautla, the city of Querétaro, and the Pacific coast from Acapulco to Zacatula. After independence it became the State of Mexico, from which the Federal District and Querétaro (1824), Guerrero (1849), and Hidalgo and Morelos (1869) were later carved.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of México, Distrito Federal, Hidalgo, Morelos, Querétaro and Guerrero. Main deviations: eastern Guerrero (Tlapa and the coast east of Acapulco toward Ometepec) belonged to Puebla, and parts of the Tierra Caliente on the Balsas belonged to Valladolid; the edges in the Huasteca and Sierra Gorda (northern Hidalgo and Querétaro) differ from the modern lines. Humboldt gives its coast as 82 leagues "from Acapulco to Zacatula" and notes that near Zimapán and Meztitlán only a narrow strip of Veracruz separated it from the Gulf.

properties.title: Intendancy of Puebla (1786)
properties.label: Puebla
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Puebla was the second most populous, a region of grain farms, textile workshops and dense Nahua and Mixtec villages on the main road from Veracruz to Mexico City. It included the government of Tlaxcala until 1793 and reached the Pacific through Tlapa and Igualapa, in what is now eastern Guerrero.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Puebla and Tlaxcala. Main deviations: Tlaxcala was separated as its own government in 1793; the Pacific districts of Tlapa and Igualapa (Humboldt gives "only a coast of 26 leagues towards the Great Ocean"), now in Guerrero, are not shown; some districts later passed to Veracruz, Guerrero and Morelos.

properties.title: Intendancy of Veracruz (1786)
properties.label: Veracruz
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Veracruz was a long, thinly peopled strip of hot lowland along the Gulf from the Pánuco and Tampico to the Tabasco border, with New Spain's only port licensed for the transatlantic trade, the fortress of San Juan de Ulúa, and the healthier towns of Xalapa, Córdoba and Orizaba on the road up to the plateau. Most of New Spain's trade with Spain, and its silver, passed through the port.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Veracruz. Tabasco, a separate government, is shown on its own (see e4-tabasco), although Humboldt, writing c. 1803, counts it in this intendancy and gives its coast as 210 leagues from the bay of Términos to Tampico. Inland edges toward Puebla, Oaxaca and the Huasteca differ from the modern lines.

properties.title: Intendancy of Oaxaca (1786)
properties.label: Oaxaca
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Oaxaca, a mountainous intendancy of Zapotec, Mixtec and other indigenous communities, lived largely from cochineal, the red dye that indigenous producers raised on cactus and that was New Spain's second-largest export after silver. Alcaldes mayores had controlled the trade through forced credit (the repartimiento), which the ordinance tried to abolish.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Oaxaca, which corresponds closely; the borders with Puebla, Veracruz and Guerrero (Costa Chica) differed in detail.

properties.title: Intendancy of Mérida (Yucatán) (1786)
properties.label: Mérida (Yucatán)
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Mérida covered the Yucatán peninsula, a Maya region of maize and cattle estates linked by sea to Veracruz and Havana rather than by land to Mexico City. Its governor-intendant also commanded the coast against the British, whose logwood cutters on the Belize River were confined by the treaties of 1783 and 1786 to a defined area.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Yucatán, Campeche and Quintana Roo. The southern and eastern interior (most of Quintana Roo and southern Campeche) was barely administered, and the British logwood settlements in Belize are not represented. Tabasco, attached to Mérida for treasury purposes only from 1787, is shown separately (see e4-tabasco).

sources.citation: Áurea Commons, Las intendencias de la Nueva España (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas / Instituto de Geografía, 1993).

properties.title: Government of Tabasco (1787)
properties.label: Tabasco
properties.description: Tabasco, a low, wet province of rivers and cacao groves between Veracruz and the Yucatán peninsula, was not made an intendancy in 1786. It stayed a separate government (gobierno) whose governor answered to the viceroy and the Audiencia of Mexico in political and military matters, while from 1787 its treasury business was placed under the intendant of Mérida, for which it served as a subdelegación. This divided status explains why accounts attach it to Mérida, to Veracruz (as Humboldt did) or to neither; it became a state of its own in 1824.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Tabasco, which corresponds closely to the colonial province; the edges toward the Laguna de Términos (Campeche) and Chiapas differed in detail.

sources.citation: Francisco Luis Jiménez Abollado, "Los fondos de comunidad y las finanzas de los pueblos de indios en un área marginal: la provincia de Tabasco a fines del siglo XVIII (1793–1797)", Estudios de Cultura Maya 63 (2024).

properties.title: Intendancy of Valladolid (Michoacán) (1786)
properties.label: Valladolid (Michoacán)
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Valladolid (today Morelia) governed Michoacán, from the Lerma river and the Bajío border down through the Purépecha highlands to the hot Tepalcatepec and Balsas basins and the Pacific coast. Its farming towns, sugar haciendas and creole clergy made it a centre of the conspiracies of 1809 and of the insurgency after 1810.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Michoacán and Colima (Colima's Revillagigedo Islands are left out). Colima belonged to Valladolid at first and was transferred to Guadalajara in the 1790s (sources give dates between about 1790 and 1795). Parts of the Tierra Caliente now in Guerrero (around Coyuca and Cutzamala) belonged to Valladolid; Humboldt describes its northern limit as the Río Lerma and its Pacific coast as more than 38 leagues.

sources.citation: Áurea Commons, Las intendencias de la Nueva España (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas / Instituto de Geografía, 1993).

properties.title: Intendancy of Guanajuato (1786)
properties.label: Guanajuato
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Guanajuato was the smallest in area but one of the most densely peopled, the heart of the Bajío: the silver mines of Guanajuato (including the Valenciana) and a ring of farming and textile towns (Celaya, Salamanca, León, San Miguel el Grande). In 1810 it became the cradle of Hidalgo's rising.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Guanajuato, which descends from it almost unchanged.

sources.citation: Áurea Commons, Las intendencias de la Nueva España (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas / Instituto de Geografía, 1993).

properties.title: Intendancy of Guadalajara (1786)
properties.label: Guadalajara
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Guadalajara, the old kingdom of Nueva Galicia and seat of an audiencia, had a long Pacific coast (Humboldt gives 123 leagues) that included the new naval base of San Blas. Its capital was the main city of the west, with its own university from 1792 and a merchant guild (consulado) from 1795.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Jalisco, Nayarit and Aguascalientes. Aguascalientes was assigned to Guadalajara in 1786 but claimed by Zacatecas, to which it was attached by 1804 (sources give dates from 1789 to 1804); Colima was added from Valladolid in the 1790s. The frontier district of Colotlán and the border with Zacatecas did not follow modern lines.

properties.title: Intendancy of Zacatecas (1786)
properties.label: Zacatecas
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Zacatecas was a mining intendancy: the city of Zacatecas, Sombrerete, Fresnillo and other reales on the dry northern plateau, which revived strongly in the later eighteenth century under tax concessions to miners.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern state of Zacatecas. Aguascalientes, attached to Zacatecas by 1804, is shown with Guadalajara, to which the ordinance first assigned it. The borders with Guadalajara (Colotlán, Bolaños) and San Luis Potosí differ in detail.

properties.title: Intendancy of San Luis Potosí (1786)
properties.label: San Luis Potosí
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; San Luis Potosí was the intendancy of the northeast. Its intendant's jurisdiction covered the province of San Luis itself (with the mines of Charcas and, from the 1770s, Catorce) and the colonies of Nuevo León and Nuevo Santander, and for treasury purposes also Coahuila and Texas. Humboldt credits it with more than 230 leagues of Gulf coast.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of San Luis Potosí, Nuevo León and Tamaulipas (Nuevo Santander). Coahuila and Texas, which Humboldt counts in this intendancy but which belonged to the Provincias Internas, are shown with the latter. Nuevo Santander reached north to the Nueces river, beyond modern Tamaulipas, and Nuevo León and Nuevo Santander were themselves attached to the Provincias Internas in 1786–93 and again from 1812–13. The Huasteca edge toward Veracruz and México differs from the modern lines.

properties.title: Intendancy of Durango (1786)
properties.label: Durango
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Durango was the old province of Nueva Vizcaya, a vast region of mines (Parral, Santa Eulalia and Chihuahua), cattle ranges and missions, exposed to Apache raids from the north. Unlike the intendancies to the south, it lay inside the Provincias Internas, so its intendant answered to the commandant general in military matters.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Durango and Chihuahua. El Paso del Norte (Ciudad Juárez) belonged to New Mexico, not Nueva Vizcaya; Saltillo and Parras (now Coahuila) had been transferred from Nueva Vizcaya to Coahuila in 1785; the Bolsón de Mapimí and the far north were Apache country rather than administered territory.

properties.title: Intendancy of Arizpe (Sonora y Sinaloa) (1786)
properties.label: Arizpe (Sonora y Sinaloa)
properties.description: Created by the Real Ordenanza de Intendentes of 4 December 1786, which divided New Spain into twelve intendancies whose intendants took over justice, finance, war and public works from the old alcaldes mayores; Arizpe united the provinces of Sinaloa, Ostimuri and Sonora along the Gulf of California, and its capital, Arizpe, was also the seat of the commandant general of the Provincias Internas. Its northern edge, the Pimería Alta, included the presidios and missions of Tubac, Tumacácori, San Xavier del Bac and Tucson, now in Arizona.
properties.note: Drawn from the modern states of Sonora and Sinaloa. The Pimería Alta extended into what is now southern Arizona (shown with the Provincias Internas), while the Seri coast and the Apache frontier in the northeast were outside effective control.

properties.title: Jacinto Canek's rising at Cisteil
properties.label: Canek 1761
properties.description: At a village fiesta in Cisteil, in the Sotuta district of the Yucatán interior, the Maya Jacinto Uc de los Santos had himself crowned king as Canek ("Chichán Moctezuma"), killed a Spanish merchant and called on the surrounding villages to drive out the Spaniards. Some 1,500 rebels fortified the village around its church; on 26 November more than 500 militiamen stormed it, killing about 500 Maya, and burned the village. Canek and eight others were executed with exemplary cruelty in the main square of Mérida on 14 December.
properties.note: Marked at the site of Cisteil (Yaxcabá municipality). Gillingham (ch. 8) spells the village Quisteil and the title Chichán Montezuma. A first militia detachment under Captain Tiburcio Cosgaya was defeated on 20 November.

sources.citation: Robert W. Patch, "La rebelión de Jacinto Canek en Yucatán: una nueva interpretación", Desacatos 13 (2003): 46–59.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: José de Gálvez's general inspection (visita) of New Spain
properties.label: Gálvez's visita
properties.description: Sent by Charles III to raise revenue and tighten royal control, the visitor-general José de Gálvez reorganised the treasury, set up the tobacco monopoly, enforced the expulsion of the Jesuits, crushed the riots of 1767, and organised the Sonora campaign and the occupation of Alta California. As Minister of the Indies from 1776 he went on to create the Provincias Internas and the intendancies, the core of the Bourbon reforms in New Spain.
properties.note: Marked at the viceregal palace in Mexico City; Gálvez spent much of 1768–70 in the northwest (San Blas, Baja California and Sonora). Gillingham (ch. 8) dates Gálvez's ministry 1777–1786; he was appointed Minister of the Indies in 1776 (Navarro García) and died in office in 1787.

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Luis Navarro García, Don José de Gálvez y la Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas del Norte de Nueva España (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, Sevilla, 1964).
D. A. Brading, Miners and Merchants in Bourbon Mexico, 1763–1810 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).

properties.title: Royal tobacco monopoly and the Mexico City factory
properties.label: Tobacco factory
properties.description: The crown took over the growing, manufacture and sale of tobacco from 1765. Cigars and cigarettes were made in state factories at Mexico City, Puebla, Oaxaca, Orizaba, Querétaro and Guadalajara; by the 1790s the Mexico City factory employed several thousand men and women, one of the largest workplaces in New Spain. The monopoly became one of the crown's biggest sources of revenue in New Spain.
properties.note: Marked at La Ciudadela, the building put up for the Mexico City factory from 1793 (finished 1807); the factory worked in other premises before that. Other factories are not mapped separately.

sources.citation: Susan Deans-Smith, Bureaucrats, Planters, and Workers: The Making of the Tobacco Monopoly in Bourbon Mexico (University of Texas Press, 1992).
D. A. Brading, Miners and Merchants in Bourbon Mexico, 1763–1810 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).

properties.title: Licensed tobacco-growing district of Córdoba and Orizaba
properties.label: Tobacco district
properties.description: To control supply, the monopoly confined legal cultivation to a small area on the eastern escarpment around Córdoba and Orizaba (with Huatusco and Zongolica), where licensed growers sold their whole crop to the crown, and troops uprooted plantings elsewhere. The arrangement made the district's planters dependent on the crown as their only buyer.
properties.note: Marked at Córdoba; the licensed district covered the jurisdictions of Córdoba, Orizaba and neighbouring areas.

sources.citation: Susan Deans-Smith, Bureaucrats, Planters, and Workers: The Making of the Tobacco Monopoly in Bourbon Mexico (University of Texas Press, 1992).

properties.title: Expulsion of the Jesuits from New Spain
properties.label: Jesuits expelled
properties.description: Under Charles III's secret decree, troops surrounded the Jesuit houses of New Spain at dawn on 25 June 1767, starting with the Colegio Máximo of San Pedro y San Pablo in Mexico City. Several hundred Jesuits were marched to Veracruz and shipped by way of Havana and Spain into exile in Italy, and the order's colleges, haciendas and northern missions were confiscated. The expulsion removed many creole teachers and set off some of the most serious riots of the colonial period.
properties.note: Marked at the former Jesuit church of San Pedro y San Pablo (now the Museo de las Constituciones), part of the Colegio Máximo. Gillingham (ch. 8) gives 678 Jesuits expelled.
properties.modern_place: Museo de las Constituciones, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).

properties.title: The Jesuits leave Baja California
properties.label: Loreto 1768
properties.description: In Baja California, where the Jesuits had run the missions since 1697, the new governor Gaspar de Portolá gathered the missionaries at Loreto and shipped them out in February 1768. The missions passed to the Franciscans under Junípero Serra, and in 1773 to the Dominicans, while the Franciscans moved north to Alta California.

sources.citation: Harry W. Crosby, Antigua California: Mission and Colony on the Peninsular Frontier, 1697–1768 (University of New Mexico Press, 1994).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Riots of 1767 in San Luis Potosí
properties.label: San Luis Potosí 1767
properties.description: Miners from Cerro de San Pedro and people from the surrounding villages took over San Luis Potosí in a series of riots from May 1767, protesting among other things new taxes, the ban on carrying arms and the expulsion of vagrants, and in June trying to stop the Jesuits' departure. Gálvez arrived with troops and punished the rebels with mass trials, executions and banishments that were meant as an example to the rest of New Spain.
properties.modern_place: San Luis Potosí, San Luis Potosí, Mexico

sources.citation: Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).

properties.title: Riot at San Luis de la Paz
properties.label: San Luis de la Paz 1767
properties.description: In this Chichimec and Otomí town at the edge of the Sierra Gorda, long a Jesuit mission, the inhabitants drove out the officials sent to expel their missionaries in June 1767 and rioted again in July. It was the first place Gálvez punished on his tour of repression: four ringleaders were executed on 20 July.
properties.modern_place: San Luis de la Paz, Guanajuato, Mexico

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Riots of 1767 in Guanajuato
properties.label: Guanajuato 1767
properties.description: Guanajuato saw six riots in a year, mostly against the collection of the tribute and the sales tax and the new tobacco monopoly, and in July 1767 against the expulsion of the Jesuits, when the crowd stoned the parish priest who tried to calm it. Gálvez arrived in October, and on 6 November sentenced nine ringleaders to death and some 180 others to flogging, prison or banishment.

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Riots of 1767 in Michoacán
properties.label: Pátzcuaro 1767
properties.description: Purépecha towns around Pátzcuaro and Uruapan had resisted the new militia levies since 1766, and in May 1767 followers of Pátzcuaro's indigenous governor, Pedro de Soria Villarroel, freed him from jail. About 460 of his supporters were seized by a ruse and tried at Valladolid, where Gálvez in November had Soria and others executed and their heads displayed over their homes.
properties.note: Marked at Pátzcuaro; the unrest spread across several towns of the Michoacán highlands, and the trials were held in Valladolid.

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Gálvez's punitive tour of 1767
properties.label: Gálvez 1767
properties.description: With full powers from Viceroy Croix and an escort of troops, Gálvez spent four and a half months touring the rebellious districts and holding summary trials. By Priestley's count, 85 people were executed, 73 flogged, 674 sentenced to prison and 117 banished; the towns had to pay for new militia companies. The campaign showed both the reach of the new Bourbon state and how much resentment it stirred.
properties.note: Main stops only, in the order documented by Priestley: Mexico City (left 9 July), San Luis de la Paz (to 21 July), San Luis Potosí (to 11 October), Guanajuato (16 October–11 November), Valladolid (from 14 November), and back to Mexico City on 24 November. The roads between them are not shown. Gillingham (ch. 8) gives eighty executions. He also lists "1767 in Guadalajara" among the three great urban riots of the colony; the sources used here, and his own account of 1767, place the risings in San Luis Potosí, Guanajuato, Michoacán and San Luis de la Paz, and no Guadalajara riot is mapped.

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Felipe Castro Gutiérrez, Nueva ley y nuevo rey: reformas borbónicas y rebelión popular en Nueva España (El Colegio de Michoacán / Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1996).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: The Sonora expedition against the Seris and Pimas
properties.label: Sonora expedition
properties.description: Gálvez sent a military expedition under Colonel Domingo Elizondo by sea to Guaymas to subdue the Seris and rebel Pimas, who had held out in the mountains of Cerro Prieto north of Guaymas. After years of costly campaigning, the rebels surrendered in stages by 1771. Gálvez himself went to Sonora in 1769 and fell seriously ill there.
properties.note: Marked at Guaymas, the expedition's base; the fighting took place mainly in the Cerro Prieto mountains between Guaymas and Pitic (Hermosillo).

sources.citation: Ignacio del Río, La aplicación regional de las reformas borbónicas en Nueva España: Sonora y Sinaloa, 1768–1787 (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1995).
Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
Luis Navarro García, Don José de Gálvez y la Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas del Norte de Nueva España (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, Sevilla, 1964).

properties.title: Naval base of San Blas
properties.label: San Blas
properties.description: Gálvez established a shipyard and port at San Blas, on the Pacific coast of Nueva Galicia, to supply Sonora, the Californias and later the expeditions to the Pacific Northwest. Ships from San Blas carried the supplies that kept the Alta California missions and presidios alive, and in 1789 the expedition that occupied Nootka Sound, which led to a crisis with Britain.
properties.note: Sources give 1767 (first works), 1768 (formal establishment) or later dates for the naval department.

sources.citation: Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Portolá expedition from San Diego to San Francisco Bay
properties.label: Portolá 1769
properties.description: With Russian traders active in Alaska, Gálvez ordered the occupation of San Diego and Monterey, sending two ships and two land parties from Baja California. From San Diego the governor, Gaspar de Portolá, led some sixty men north along the coast to find Monterey Bay, passed it without recognising it, and in early November reached the hills above San Francisco Bay, the first Europeans known to have seen it. The party returned to San Diego in January 1770.
properties.note: Main stops only (San Diego, the Los Angeles basin, the Santa Barbara Channel, San Luis Obispo, Monterey Bay, Santa Cruz, Sweeney Ridge); the line follows the coast between them. The scouts under Sergeant Ortega saw the bay on about 1–2 November and the whole party on 4 November.

sources.citation: David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Herbert Ingram Priestley, José de Gálvez, Visitor-General of New Spain (1765–1771) (University of California Press, 1916).

properties.title: Presidio and mission of San Diego
properties.label: San Diego 1769
properties.description: Junípero Serra founded the mission of San Diego de Alcalá on Presidio Hill, beside the camp of the expedition, the first of the 21 Franciscan missions of Alta California. The mission moved to its present site up the San Diego River valley in 1774.
properties.note: Marked at Presidio Hill (Presidio Park), the site of the presidio and the first mission.

sources.citation: David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Presidio and mission of Monterey
properties.label: Monterey 1770
properties.description: On a second attempt Portolá and Serra recognised Monterey Bay and founded the presidio and the mission of San Carlos Borromeo there; the mission moved to Carmel the next year. Monterey became the capital of Alta California.
properties.note: Marked at the Royal Presidio Chapel (San Carlos Cathedral), the surviving building of the presidio.

sources.citation: David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Line of presidios under the Reglamento of 1772
properties.label: Presidio line 1772
properties.description: After the Marqués de Rubí's inspection of the frontier (1766–68), the royal regulation of September 1772 ordered a cordon of fifteen presidios about forty leagues apart from Altar, near the head of the Gulf of California, to La Bahía del Espíritu Santo on the Texas coast, with Santa Fe and San Antonio outside the line. Hugo O'Conor relocated most of them between 1773 and 1775. The line traced roughly the future US–Mexico border, and it reflected a retreat to defensible positions rather than further expansion.
properties.note: An indicative line through presidios of the cordon whose sites are well known (Altar, Tubac, Fronteras, Janos, Carrizal, Julimes, San Juan Bautista del Río Grande at Guerrero, La Bahía at Goliad), not a frontier that existed on the ground. Several presidios were moved more than once (Tubac to Tucson, El Paso to Carrizal, Terrenate, Fronteras, San Sabá and others), so the line changed shape over time.

sources.citation: Max L. Moorhead, The Presidio: Bastion of the Spanish Borderlands (University of Oklahoma Press, 1975).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Luis Navarro García, Don José de Gálvez y la Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas del Norte de Nueva España (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, Sevilla, 1964).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 8 and 10.

properties.title: Los Adaes abandoned; capital of Texas moves to San Antonio
properties.label: Los Adaes 1773
properties.description: With French Louisiana ceded to Spain in 1762–63, the regulation of 1772 ordered the abandonment of Los Adaes, capital of Texas since 1729 and facing the French post of Natchitoches. About 500 people were ordered to San Antonio de Béxar, which became the capital, but most soon returned east and, after a stay at Bucareli on the Trinity, founded Nacogdoches in 1779.
properties.note: Marked at Los Adaes State Historic Site near Robeline, Louisiana.

sources.citation: James L. McCorkle Jr., "Los Adaes", Handbook of Texas Online (Texas State Historical Association).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Silver strike at Real de Catorce
properties.label: Real de Catorce
properties.description: A mining settlement was founded in 1772 in the Sierra de Catorce, high in the dry north of the San Luis Potosí intendancy, and a rich vein found there in 1773 started one of the great silver booms of the late colony, with dozens of mines registered by the early 1780s. Catorce and the Valenciana show how the reduced mercury prices and tax concessions of the Bourbon reforms helped silver output reach its colonial peak around 1800.
properties.modern_place: Real de Catorce, San Luis Potosí, Mexico

sources.citation: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia, "Real de Catorce", Lugares INAH.
D. A. Brading, Miners and Merchants in Bourbon Mexico, 1763–1810 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 6.

properties.title: The Valenciana silver mine
properties.label: La Valenciana
properties.description: Antonio de Obregón y Alcocer, who had worked an abandoned vein north of Guanajuato for years, struck rich ore in the late 1760s; the Valenciana grew into one of the richest silver mines in the world, and Obregón was made Count of Valenciana in 1780. With several thousand workers and a shaft hundreds of metres deep, it helped make Guanajuato the leading silver district of New Spain, as Humboldt found when he visited in 1803.
properties.note: Marked at the Valenciana church beside the mine. Gillingham (ch. 4) calls the neighbouring Rayas mine, on the same vein, the largest in the world around 1800; Humboldt and Brading treat the Valenciana as the richest.

sources.citation: D. A. Brading, Miners and Merchants in Bourbon Mexico, 1763–1810 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).
Alexander von Humboldt, Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain, trans. John Black, 4 vols. (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme and Brown, 1811).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 4 and 6.

properties.title: Real del Monte: the Count of Regla and the strike of 1766
properties.label: Real del Monte
properties.description: Pedro Romero de Terreros, a Querétaro shopkeeper's nephew, spent a fortune draining the flooded Veta Vizcaína above Pachuca and made it one of the richest mines in the world. When he cut wages and the miners' traditional share of the ore (the partido), the workers struck in July 1766, and on 15 August a crowd fatally stoned the district magistrate and killed a mine foreman. The viceroy's mining expert Francisco de Gamboa drew up new rules, but the dispute dragged on for years. Romero was made Count of Regla in 1768, gave the king warships, and in 1775 founded the Monte de Piedad, the pawnbroking charity on Mexico City's main square.
properties.note: Marked at the town of Real del Monte (Mineral del Monte); the Vizcaína mines and the San Cayetano mine where the magistrate was attacked lie close by. Gillingham (chs. 4, 6 and 8) does not name the strike, but describes Romero driving his workers to rebellion and calls the Vizcaína "Pachuca's".

sources.citation: Doris M. Ladd, The Making of a Strike: Mexican Silver Workers' Struggles in Real del Monte, 1766–1775 (University of Nebraska Press, 1988).
Edith Boorstein Couturier, The Silver King: The Remarkable Life of the Count of Regla in Colonial Mexico (University of New Mexico Press, 2003).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 4, 6 and 8.

properties.title: Presidio of San Agustín del Tucson
properties.label: Tucson 1775
properties.description: Hugo O'Conor chose a site beside the O'odham village of Cuk Ṣon, on the Santa Cruz River, to replace the presidio of Tubac, and the garrison moved there in 1776. It anchored the northern edge of Sonora's Pimería Alta and is the origin of modern Tucson.
properties.note: Marked at the centre of Tucson; the presidio stood in what is now downtown.

sources.citation: John L. Kessell, Friars, Soldiers, and Reformers: Hispanic Arizona and the Sonora Mission Frontier, 1767–1856 (University of Arizona Press, 1976).
Max L. Moorhead, The Presidio: Bastion of the Spanish Borderlands (University of Oklahoma Press, 1975).

properties.title: Anza's colonizing expedition to San Francisco Bay
properties.label: Anza 1775–76
properties.description: Juan Bautista de Anza, captain of Tubac, had opened an overland route from Sonora to California in 1774. In 1775–76 he led about 240 settlers, soldiers' families among them, with a large herd of cattle, from Tubac down the Gila, across the Colorado at the Yuma crossing and the desert, to San Gabriel and Monterey. In March 1776 he chose the sites for the presidio and mission of San Francisco, and the colonists arrived there in June.
properties.note: Main stops only: Tubac, San Xavier del Bac, Tucson, the Gila villages near Sacaton, Gila Bend, the Yuma crossing, Coyote Canyon near Borrego Springs, San Gabriel, San Luis Obispo, Monterey and San Francisco. Many colonists had gathered earlier at Culiacán and San Miguel de Horcasitas. Anza himself returned from Monterey; the colonists continued under Lieutenant José Joaquín Moraga.

sources.citation: Herbert Eugene Bolton, ed., Anza's California Expeditions, 5 vols. (University of California Press, 1930).
US National Park Service, Juan Bautista de Anza National Historic Trail, "History & Culture".
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Presidio and mission of San Francisco
properties.label: San Francisco 1776
properties.description: Anza's colonists under Moraga founded the presidio on the Golden Gate on 17 September 1776, and the mission of San Francisco de Asís (Mission Dolores) followed in October, the northern outpost of Spanish settlement on the Pacific coast.

sources.citation: Herbert Eugene Bolton, ed., Anza's California Expeditions, 5 vols. (University of California Press, 1930).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Arizpe, capital of the Provincias Internas
properties.label: Arizpe
properties.description: Teodoro de Croix reached the Sonoran river town of Arizpe in late 1779 and proclaimed it the capital of the Provincias Internas in January 1780. It lay far from the Apache and Comanche frontiers of Chihuahua, Coahuila and Texas; the western commanders kept it as their seat after the divisions of 1786–87, but Pedro de Nava moved the headquarters of the reunited command to Chihuahua in 1793.

sources.citation: Luis Navarro García, Don José de Gálvez y la Comandancia General de las Provincias Internas del Norte de Nueva España (Escuela de Estudios Hispano-Americanos, Sevilla, 1964).
Peter Gerhard, The North Frontier of New Spain, rev. ed. (University of Oklahoma Press, 1993).

properties.title: Quechan (Yuma) revolt at the Colorado crossing
properties.label: Yuma revolt 1781
properties.description: Spain founded two mission-pueblos among the Quechans at the Colorado–Gila crossing in 1780–81 to guard Anza's road. Angered by settlers' livestock in their fields and broken promises, the Quechans destroyed both settlements, killing dozens of soldiers, settlers and friars, among them Captain Fernando Rivera y Moncada and Father Francisco Garcés, and carrying off women and children. The overland route to California was effectively closed for the rest of the colonial period, leaving the province dependent on ships from San Blas.
properties.note: Marked at the hill of the Purísima Concepción settlement (later Fort Yuma), on the California bank opposite Yuma; the second settlement, San Pedro y San Pablo de Bicuñer, lay a few miles upstream. Death tolls in the literature range from about 50 to more than 100.

sources.citation: Mark Santiago, Massacre at the Yuma Crossing: Spanish Relations with the Quechans, 1779–1782 (University of Arizona Press, 1998).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Founding of the pueblo of Los Ángeles
properties.label: Los Ángeles 1781
properties.description: Governor Felipe de Neve founded two civilian farming towns to feed the California presidios, San José (1777) and Los Ángeles, settled by eleven families, most of mixed African, indigenous and Spanish ancestry, recruited in Sinaloa and Sonora.
properties.note: Marked at the Plaza; the first settlement stood a little away from the present plaza.

sources.citation: David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).

properties.title: Anza's peace with the Comanches
properties.label: Comanche peace 1786
properties.description: As governor of New Mexico, Anza defeated the Comanche leader Cuerno Verde in 1779 and then negotiated a lasting peace with Ecueracapa, spokesman of the western Comanches, concluded at Pecos in February 1786. The Comanches gained access to New Mexican trade fairs and joined Spain against the Apaches; the peace held for decades and reshaped the balance of power on the southern Plains.
properties.note: Marked at Pecos Pueblo, where the agreement was concluded according to most accounts; talks were also held at Santa Fe and Taos.

sources.citation: Pekka Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (Yale University Press, 2008).
David J. Weber, The Spanish Frontier in North America (Yale University Press, 1992).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 10.

properties.title: Merchant guild (consulado) of Veracruz
properties.label: Consulado of Veracruz
properties.description: The "free trade" regulation of 1778, extended to New Spain in 1789, opened trade with more Spanish ports and weakened the hold of the Mexico City merchant guild over imports. By royal cédula of 17 January 1795 the crown created a consulado at Veracruz (installed that April), and another at Guadalajara in June, giving the port merchants their own commercial court and funds, which went partly into public works such as the road up to Xalapa and Perote.
properties.note: Marked at the city of Veracruz. The dates are from Souto Mantecón (2006).

sources.citation: Matilde Souto Mantecón, "Creación y disolución de los consulados de comercio de la Nueva España", Revista Complutense de Historia de América 32 (2006): 19–39.
D. A. Brading, Miners and Merchants in Bourbon Mexico, 1763–1810 (Cambridge University Press, 1971).

properties.title: Smallpox riot at Teotitlán del Valle
properties.label: Teotitlán 1796
properties.description: When smallpox reached this Zapotec weaving town near Antequera (Oaxaca) in 1796, the intendant closed its roads, took the sick to a new infirmary outside the town and ordered them buried in a separate cemetery rather than at the church. After the first death in the infirmary, residents forced a church burial, and on 8 October a crowd, led largely by women, stormed the infirmary and carried the sick home. Grenadiers were sent in and the patients returned, but the authorities turned increasingly to persuasion and inoculation. The episode shows how Bourbon public-health measures collided with village custom.
properties.note: The outcome is told differently: Gillingham (ch. 8), following Ramírez, says nobody was seriously punished and the town won its main demands; Aguilera-Núñez reports that the ringleaders were flogged and jailed and the quarantine was kept.

sources.citation: Ana-Rosalía Aguilera-Núñez, "La epidemia de viruela de 1796-1797 en Oaxaca (México): variolización, discursos, (re)acciones e impacto demográfico", HiSTOReLo. Revista de Historia Regional y Local 15, no. 34 (2023): 167–204.
Paul Ramírez, "'Like Herod's Massacre': Quarantines, Bourbon Reform, and Popular Protest in Oaxaca's Smallpox Epidemic, 1796–1797", The Americas 69, no. 2 (2012): 203–235.
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Humboldt's journey through New Spain
properties.label: Humboldt 1803–04
properties.description: The Prussian scientist Alexander von Humboldt and Aimé Bonpland landed at Acapulco, crossed the Sierra to Taxco and Mexico City, studied the mines of Real del Monte and Guanajuato, climbed the young volcano of Jorullo, and left from Veracruz a year later. His Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain (1808–11), built on the viceroyalty's own statistics, described its intendancies, mines and inequality and gave Europe and Mexico's founders a picture of a vast, rich country.
properties.note: Main stops only: Acapulco, Chilpancingo, Taxco, Cuernavaca, Mexico City, Guanajuato, Valladolid, Pátzcuaro, Jorullo, Toluca, back to Mexico City, then Puebla, Perote, Xalapa and Veracruz. Excursions from Mexico City (Real del Monte, the Valley of Mexico) are omitted, and the roads between stops are not traced.

sources.citation: Alexander von Humboldt, Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain, trans. John Black, 4 vols. (London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, Orme and Brown, 1811).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), chs. 6 and 8.

properties.title: Consolidación de Vales Reales
properties.label: Consolidación 1804
properties.description: To pay for its wars, the crown ordered church charitable funds, which had been lent out as mortgages across New Spain, to be called in and remitted to Spain. Thousands of landowners, miners and merchants who owed these loans were forced to repay or lose their property, alienating much of creole society and the lower clergy. New Spain sent more than any other part of the empire before the measure was suspended in 1808.
properties.note: A measure applied throughout New Spain; marked at Mexico City, seat of the Junta Superior de Consolidación.
properties.modern_place: Plaza de la Constitución, Ciudad de México

sources.citation: Gisela von Wobeser, Dominación colonial: la consolidación de vales reales en Nueva España, 1804–1812 (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 2003).
Brian R. Hamnett, Roots of Insurgency: Mexican Regions, 1750–1824 (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Coup against Viceroy Iturrigaray
properties.label: Coup of 1808
properties.description: When Napoleon forced the Spanish Bourbons to abdicate, the creole-led city council of Mexico City proposed a provisional government in the name of Ferdinand VII, and Viceroy José de Iturrigaray seemed to sympathise. On the night of 15 September 1808 peninsular merchants led by Gabriel de Yermo seized the viceroy in his palace, arrested the leading autonomists and installed the elderly field marshal Pedro Garibay as viceroy. By closing the legal path to self-government, the coup pushed creoles toward conspiracy and, two years later, rebellion.

sources.citation: Timothy E. Anna, The Fall of the Royal Government in Mexico City (University of Nebraska Press, 1978).
Virginia Guedea, En busca de un gobierno alterno: los Guadalupes de México (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1992).
Gisela von Wobeser, Dominación colonial: la consolidación de vales reales en Nueva España, 1804–1812 (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, Instituto de Investigaciones Históricas, 2003).
Paul Gillingham, Mexico: A 500-Year History (Atlantic Monthly Press, 2025), ch. 8.

properties.title: Conspiracy of Valladolid
properties.label: Valladolid 1809
properties.description: Creole officers and lawyers in Valladolid, led by José María García Obeso and José Mariano Michelena, planned to set up a junta to govern in the name of the captive king, counting on support from the indigenous towns. The plot was betrayed and broken up on 21 December 1809, but its leaders were treated leniently, and several of its ideas reappeared in the Querétaro conspiracy that started the rising of 1810.

sources.citation: Virginia Guedea, En busca de un gobierno alterno: los Guadalupes de México (Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, 1992).
Brian R. Hamnett, Roots of Insurgency: Mexican Regions, 1750–1824 (Cambridge University Press, 1986).
